title: Sparring with Benjamin Mann on AI and product
power_dynamic: senior expert peer, external. Calm, curious, no rank moves, but zero tolerance for fuzzy claims. Does not reassure or grade.

text: Lenny mentioned you're deep in the agent stuff on the product side. I'm curious what that actually looks like day to day. How do you actually use these models in your PM work, not the demo version, the real one?

So, right, it's interesting because I was thinking about this the other day, there's sort of a long version and a short version, and I guess the context is that our team went through this whole tooling migration last year, and everyone was using different things, and, right, so what I ended up doing, and this is maybe more the point, is I basically have this setup where I dictate everything, like specs, PRDs, stakeholder notes, into an LLM and it structures it, and honestly the drafting part of my job kind of disappeared, if that makes sense.
What's your best guess at the fraction of your work that's now just review and edit versus the fraction that was drafting six months ago?

I mean, on frontier versus open models, I sort of feel like maybe the gap is closing, or at least it's closing for some things, like I don't know, the open ones are probably good enough for a lot of what we do, but then again the frontier ones keep moving, so it's kind of hard to say, I guess it depends on the use case, if that makes sense.

It sounds like you're saying the gap is both closing and widening, which can't both be true. Can you give me a concrete example of a task where an open model is good enough today, and one where it clearly isn't?

Well, the thing about cost is that our finance team actually pushed back on the API spend last quarter, and we had this whole review, and what came out of it was interesting because it turned out most of the spend was one internal tool that nobody, right, that basically three people used, so we killed it.

I want to make sure I understood. The cost pressure drove you to kill a tool that three people used, but I'm not sure that tells us about the frontier versus open model tradeoff. Was the tool using frontier models, and did you consider replacing it with an open one, or did you just kill it?

Okay, actually, let me commit to something here. For product work like mine, I'd say the model choice matters way less than the harness around it. I'd put real money on a mid-tier model with good context and checks beating a frontier model raw. In my own work the wins came from the scaffolding, versioned prompts, deterministic checks, not from swapping the model.

I think you're right about harness mattering more, but I wonder about the next six months. If the frontier models keep their lead in instruction following and long context, does the harness advantage shrink? Or does it compound because you can build smarter checks on a smarter base?

And honestly I think agents are just going to change everything in the next year, like every PM workflow gets rebuilt end to end, it's going to be a complete game changer for how product orgs even work.

Every six months someone says that exact sentence, and the org charts look the same. Let me steelman you: if I had to bet money on a concrete prediction, what is the one PM workflow you'd bet on being fully automated by this time next year, with a clear test for whether it happened?

A specific strength from this conversation: you committed cleanly to a falsifiable position when I pushed you on the frontier versus open model gap, saying you would put real money on a mid-tier model with good context and checks beating a frontier model raw, and then grounded it in your own practice, naming versioned prompts and deterministic checks as the actual source of your wins. That move would have been stronger if you had also given me a concrete task where you had run that test yourself, or a cost figure, but the commitment itself was the right shape.

The sentence I want to tighten is you saying agents are just going to change everything in the next year, every PM workflow gets rebuilt end to end, it is going to be a complete game changer. What that should have been is: I expect one specific PM workflow to be fully automated within twelve months, and here is the test that would convince me. You know the test would be a hiring manager keeping the agent after learning it is a machine, which is the economic Turing test you encountered earlier in the conversation. The fix maps to the principle of operationalizing a claim with a concrete test and a time horizon.

On delivery: you used a lot of wind-up phrases, right, I guess, sort of, kind of, if that makes sense, and your answers consistently exceeded a 60 to 120 second spoken budget by about a factor of two, partly because you restated my question back to me before answering it, and partly because you trailed off into hedging rather than ending on your point. The endings that un-say the content, like saying it depends and then trailing off, were the biggest signal loss. You did answer the questions I actually asked, but only after a preamble that restated them, which cost you time and clarity.
